alt: A two-by-two grid of quantity against quality. Few weak pieces, such as one rumour, fail; many weak pieces, such as ten anecdotes, still fail; one strong study of 5,000 people compensates only up to a point; several strong, independent pieces give apt support.
caption: Sufficient means enough of the right kind for this particular claim.

after: ## The scope of the claim sets the standard
alt: A staircase of claims about the timetable, rising in what they demand: “some pupils” needs a few cases; “most pupils” needs a representative sample; “causes” needs evidence of cause; “worst in the country” needs a comparison; “all pupils” is almost impossible to support. Below, a narrowed claim is easier to defend.
caption: Narrow the claim to what the evidence can support.

alt: Seven numbered cards list how evidence falls short: too little, unrepresentative, irrelevant, out of date, from an unreliable source, of only one type, or left unexplained. An eighth card warns that too much can also bury the strongest example.
caption: Check quantity, representativeness, relevance, currency, source, variety and explanation.

after: ## Sufficiency depends on the audience too
alt: Four audiences ranked by how much evidence they need: one already inclined to agree needs less, a general audience a clear example and trusted statistic, a specialist audience rigorous sources, and a sceptical or hostile audience more and more varied evidence. A side note recommends several types of evidence when resistance is likely.
caption: A sceptical audience needs more, and more varied, evidence than a friendly one.

alt: Before: a claim that phones should be banned in all schools rests on two anecdotes, leaving a wide gap. After: the claim is narrowed to lessons and supported by a study of 12 schools, a survey of 90 teachers and a concession, closing the gap.
caption: Narrow the claim and strengthen the evidence until they meet.

after: ## A public-domain example: "Let Facts be submitted"
alt: Two panels. A single grievance is one point with no direction, insufficient for a broad claim. Dozens of “He has...” grievances line up into a pattern, which is what the Declaration’s claim about a design of despotism asserts. The framing sentence “let Facts be submitted to a candid world” signals awareness that proof is needed.
caption: Only a series of related acts can show the pattern a broad claim asserts.
